(Para 201)
The Committee was also informed that the limited water front is an impediment to the
future expansion of the Port. The Port, with a total land area of 2,290 acres, presently has a
capacity of 15 berths and one SPM is already saturated. This greatly limits the ability of the Port

68
to expand in terms of infrastructure. The Committee recommends that studies must be conducted
to find a solution to the logistical and infrastructural bottlenecks that the Mangalore Portfaces,
to ensure that the future growth and expansion of the Port is done in a scientific and systematic
manner. (Para 202)
CRUSE TERMINAL
The Committee notes the steps taken by the Port to augment the facilities in terms of
Cruise tourism. Mangalore, with its beautiful coast and pristine beaches, is ideal as a cruise
destination. The Committee recommends that more must be done to fulfill the potential of the
Port as a major cruise terminal and a gateway to Peninsular India. In terms of infrastructure,
draft levels must be maintained to facilitate the participation of major cruise liners. The Committee
further recommends that the Ministry of Shipping and the NMPT should work together with the
Ministry of Tourism, tour operators and the respective State Tourism Boards to promote New
Mangalore Port as a cruise terminal. Simultaneously, the Ministry of Shipping and NMPT must
ensure that the facilities at the passenger terminals must be at par with global standards.
(Para 205)
Nestled amidst the Western Ghats in peninsular India, construction of roads and railway
lines to connect the Port, is fraught with geographical obstacles. As a result, this has reduced
the popularity of the Port due to the relatively high transportation costs and time taken. The
Committee recommends that given the availability of advanced technology, new technology and
research must be harnessed to devise a way to circumvent the geographical bottlenecks that ail
the Port. (Para 206)
While most Major Ports in India are suffering from congestion, the New Mangalore Port is
struggling to achieve even 50 per cent of its capacity utilization. The only lifeline between the
New Mangalore Port and its hinterland is the rail line provided by the Hassan- Mangalore Rail
Development Company Ltd. (HMRDC). Rail cargo has remained consistent at 7 lakh MT in the
last two financial years, indicating a case of stagnancy. The Committee recommends that the
Government may consider improving rail connectivity with NMPT. (Para 207)
Karnataka has 8 minor ports- Kundapura, Honnavar, Belekeri, Tadri, Bhatkal, Hangarakatta,
Malpe and Padubidri. These are located on the State's 300 km coastline. Hence, coastal shipping
would and should be an ideal alternative to the lack of proper road connectivity. However, the
shared hinterland implies competition for the same cargo. Also, this mode of transportation
continues to remain unexplored. Coast-to-coast mode of transportation can change the fortunes
of Indian marine logistics. It is a pity that its potential remains untapped. The example of China
may be studied, where the Chinese Government is using its coastline to connect one city to
another. This mode of transportation has proven to be cost effective and can result in faster
movement of consignments. (Para 208)
MORMUGAO PORT TRUST
PERFORMANCE
The Committee notes the efforts of the MPT in increasing the efficiency of the Port, given
the constraints imposed on the Port. The Committee understands the need for development of
infrastructure of the port. The Committee was informed by various stakeholders of the shipping

69
industry in Goa that there is an urgent need for improvement in the rail and road connectivity
in MPT in order to ensure faster evacuation of cargo, better connectivity to the hinterland and
avoid the movement of vehicles carrying cargo through congested city roads. They emphasized
the need to make the amenities given to cruise tourists at par with global standards. They
stressed on the need for doubling of railway line in Mormugao Port. The stakeholders also
highlighted the need to compensate the Port for any monetary loss that the Port might incur for
the grant of any concessional tariff for the promotion of cruise tourism. They impressed upon
the need to ensure that the facilities provided with regards to Cruise Tourism are made world
class so as to imprint a good image of Goa in the minds of the tourists. (Para 215)
Given the popularity of Goa as an international tourist destination, the Committee
recommends that the MPT should realign its focus at developing itself as a Passenger Port,
catering to Cruise Ships. Tours and Packages for the same must be worked out with the Ministry
of Tourism and the Ministry of Shipping. Necessary infrastructural requirements must be developed
in order to harness the full potential of the Port as a Passenger Port. This will ensure that the
Port is maintained as a profitable and viable venture whilst ensuring the preservation of the
environment in keeping with the orders of the Supreme Court. (Para 216)
MAJOR ISSUES AILING CARGO MANAGEMENT IN THE MAJOR PORTS
CONTAINER TRAFFIC
The Committee is of the opinion that existing and new ports should align their capacity
expansion in line with the projected increase in coastal shipping volumes. Provision of a dedicated
berth for coastal shipping should also be looked into in order to promote coastal shipping.
(Para 219)
DRAFT LIMITATIONS
The Committee has observed that the relatively low draft at Indian ports do not measure
upto internationally set standards. Presently, vessels greater than 11,000 TEU are in service. The
movement towards larger ships is driven by economies of scale. It follows that in case of
containership for 1,000 TEU capacities, the average draft is 8.3 metres, which increases to 15.5
metres for ships above 11,000 TEU capacities. Container vessels with a capacity of 4,000 TEU
requires a minimum draft of 12.5 metres. (Para 223)
The Committee feels that there is a need to maximize the utilization of these vessels, which
will in turn lead to reduction in the number of port calls on major routes and push for the
development of global mega ports served by fully integrated global network. Most Major Ports
in India have minimum draft under 12m, except for a few of the younger ports which have draft
of more than 14m. Insufficient draft at Indian Ports leads to increased costs and time taken as
cargo originating from and those that are bound for India gets routed through transshipment
ports like Colombo and Singapore. The Committee feels that as vessels keep getting bigger,
Indian ports need deeper drafts, which call for increased and greater investments in capital
dredging. (Para 224)
The Committee recommends that new terminals at Tuticorin, Ennore etc. must be developed
with a renewed zeal and vigour in a careful and strategic manner, so that they will act as active
competitors to operational container ports in Sri Lanka. (Para 225)

70
ROLE OF TARIFF REGULATIONS AT INDIA'S MAJOR PORTS
The Committee feels that the Port sector in India is facing certain tariff- related uncertainties
due to multiplicity of regimes. The non-Major Ports do not come under any tariff jurisdiction and
price their services based on market and competition. But the major ones (including private
terminals therein) fall under the jurisdiction of a regulator viz., Tariff Authority for Major Ports
(TAMP). This anomaly and the lack of a level playing field have long been a debated issue.
(Para 227)
In view of the considerable loss of business opportunities for the Major Ports due to the
provision of certain tariff related uncertainties as ascertained by TAMP, the Committee
recommends that the anomalies in the TAMP rules must be made reasonable in order to make
it lucrative for ships to call on Major Ports against private ports. The Committee further
recommends that the role of the TAMP must be redefined and that a strategic and market
oriented system of tariff must be set in place. (Para 229)
EFFICIENCY OF THE PORT SECTOR OPERATIONS
The Committee feels that low productivity and high vessel turnaround time at Indian ports
are due to: (i) Low level of mechanisation and insufficient draft; (ii) Skewed handling capacity
for different types of cargo; and (iii) Infrastructure constraints in hinterland connectivity. It has
been observed that lagging behind other countries on performance parameters pushes up the cost
of trade and renders Indian ports less competitive. Non-Major Ports have fared well, ensuring
quicker turnaround by investing in the infrastructure to handle larger vessels. Considering the
strategic location of India's Major Ports and their importance to trade, there is an opportunity
to improve their performance to meet global benchmarks. Most of the Major Ports have high
Turnaround Times even while the utilisation level is low and only a few have the ability to handle
bigger cape-size vessels. The shipping industry is moving towards cape-size vessels. So, it is
important that India develops cape handling capability at its key ports to ensure economies of
scale for the trade. (Para 231)
The Committee feels that the seaports are the interface between two modes of transport
viz., land and sea and recommends that its efficiency is directly related to the connectivity
covering both the modes of transport and as such, Container terminals should provide rapid
transit facilities for containerized cargo (similar to an Airport where passengers arrive and depart
with ready luggage/cargo). This would enable the Ports to plan and utilize land optimally for the
benefit of the ships and not for storage for which CFS / ICD are planned. (Para 234)
AUTOMATION/DIGITISATION OF PORT MANAGEMENT
The Committee feels that traffic congestion at port gates is another critical problem as it
presently has little or no automation. The entry and exit of vehicles and drivers through the
gates of container terminal should be automated. In this regard, the Committee recommends
that Optical Character Recognition (OCR) system can be installed at the terminal gates and
driver's biometric identity and their authentication documents could be stored in a smart card
which he can flash at the counter to gain entry. Furthermore, it would also be useful to implement

71
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions which are driven by an integrated suite of software
that supports the basic internal business process of any organisation. More importantly, a Port
Community System (PCS), in terms of a single technology-based platform, which will bring
together all stakeholders and shares information is essential. An 'e-custom' solution could also
be developed later. While implementation of PCS has been already initiated, its rollout has not
been very successful. Thus, before embarking on such plans, focus should be on building the
foundation and developing stakeholder capabilities. (Para 241)
EMERGING CONSTELLATION OF CONTAINER TERMINALS IN SOUTH INDIA
The Committee is of the view that more ports do not necessarily bring in more cargo. The
extent of a country's EXIM trade is a function of its policies and its openness to international
commerce. A cost-effective way of augmenting port capacity to meet demand is to upgrade
capacity of existing ports. Certainly, public investment is needed to augment port capacity. But,
a careful choice needs to be made in choosing investment between major and non-Major Ports.
(Para 245)
Investment in smaller new ports in India can yield much better returns as they would
service vessels on coastal and inland waterway. The Committee feels that the three ports coming
up within a distance of about 130 nautical miles, need to be developed and strategised in such
a manner that all the three receive sufficient cargo to ensure profitable operations. The Committee
thus recommends that infrastructure development of one port should not be at the cost of the
development of another nearby port. (Para 246)
The Committee recommends that efforts must be concentrated on the development and
expansion of infrastructure that would make water transport more attractive, instead of prioritizing
road transport and turn already over-crowded highways into death traps. More emphasis must be
placed on the coast route and inland waterways as a mode of transport for hinterland cargo
connectivity and its development must be made a priority. (Para 247)
CARGO EV ACUATION FROM INDIAN PORTS IN TERMS OF TRANSPORT MODE
The Committee, in this regard, recommends that ports must continuously take measures
to help their shipping lines and other partners within the port system to battle increased competition
and adjust to new trends in world trade. Dedicated Freight Corridors hold key to intermodal
transport and hence need to be completed on priority basis. Moreover, the inland waterways
system needs to be renovated as cargo evacuation by water is cheaper and cleaner, which reduces
costs and port congestion and brings in efficiency.  The shifting of cargo from road to train and
waterways will be environment-friendly and will also help to lower carbon emissions.
(Para 250)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and the
Ministry of Railways should ensure that all the projects linked to port connectivity be given the
highest priority and projects should be executed within the scheduled time period to make the
port operations viable and profitable. (Para 251)

72
Furthermore, the Committee recommends that evacuation of cargo to and from the port
areas have to be properly synchronized so that the inter-modal network functions smoothly. Road
and rail connectivity form an integral part of the port infrastructure as inefficient evacuation of
cargo can undermine the entire operation of a port. In particular, containerization of cargo
presupposes a seamless link with the road and rail network in an 'end to end' transport system.
Congestion at ports results in delayed evacuation of cargo due to inadequate road and rail
capacity. This adversely impacts the competitiveness of Indian industry. Port connectivity has
ramifications that go beyond the operation of a port per se. (Para 252)
There is a need to allocate the regional distribution of cargo to different modes of land
transport. Though in certain cases of bulk cargo, it is easy to identify the mode for a particular
cargo at a particular port and assumptions regarding percentage split have to be made in respect
of cargo such as POL, LPG , fertilizer, fertilizer raw material, other bulk cargo, containers and
break-bulk cargo. These assumptions need to be made depending upon the features of the
respective regions, nature of cargo, quantum of cargo and the spread of hinterland.
(Para 253)
CONTAINERIZATION
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the need of the hour is to have infrastructure
that can support seamless movement of cargo across all modes without any delay. We need to
create common user facilities where these models can be executed efficiently at a competitive
price. To harness the full potential of inter modal transport, a legal framework and financial/
regulatory incentives need to be put in place. (Para 259)
CABOTAGE LAWS
The Committee recommends that a study must be conducted on the effects of Cabotage
Laws in the shipping sector of the country. The Committee feels that research must be conducted
as to why, given the reduction of the Cabotage laws, the Ports have witnessed a paltry level of
transhipment. The policy of the Ministry in this regard must be scientifically monitored and
solutions to the same must be devised. The Committee extends its full cooperation in this matter
as it feels that the success of transshipment hubs in the country is essential for the growth of
Ports in India. (Para 261)
ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES WITH REGARDS TO COASTAL REGULATORY ZONES (CRZ) AND
NATIONAL GREEN TRIBUNAL (NGT)
The Committee feels that the development of Port infrastructure is necessary to the economic
health of the nation. Steps need to be taken to obviate the adverse impact of the order of NGT
on the port projects pending approval of the Coastal Zone Management Plan of the States by the
MoEF&CC. The Committee further recommends that the MoEF&CC must take steps to ensure
that the States/ Union Territories must take it upon themselves to prioritise the CZMPs and
submit the same to the MoEF&CC at the earliest, in order to ensure that necessary rules and
regulations may be instituted for the same. (Para 264)

73
The Committee recommends that an advisory be issued by the MoEF&CC to the States/ UTs
that have not yet submitted their CZMPs to the MoEF&CC, impressing upon them to submit
them immediately and get the same approved. The Ministry of Shipping may also take it upon
itself to ensure that it keeps a track of the same and impress upon the respective State
Governments and their corresponding ports to submit their plans at the earliest. The delay may
cost huge economic loss to the country's Shipping sector and such policy related delays should
be avoided. (Para 265)
The Committee, however, feels that coastal infrastructural projects involving wetlands include
various players whose interests will be affected in one way or another. The Committee, in this
regard, recommends that the stages included by the MoEF&CC whilst granting environmental
clearance, e.g. Expert Appraisal Committee, Public hearings, Term of Reference etc. are speeded
up to ensure that ports are getting necessary clearances without hinderances. Given the
development in science and technology, the Committee is of the opinion that effective solutions
can be found for the developmental needs of the Ports. (Para 267)
The Committee is of the opinion that many of the Major Ports are suffering due to the
absence of a Standard Operating Procedure. The Committee is dismayed to note that many of
the projects of the Major Ports have been stalled due to the same reason, while operations in
some Ports have been shut down as a result of Court orders, which could have been avoided had
these guidelines been set in place. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Shipping
must coordinate with the concerned States, the respective State Pollution Control Boards and the
MoEF&CC to formulate a set of procedures/ processes that are largely uniform across all the
States, keeping room for modifications according to the special requirements that are State or
Region specific. (Para 269)
The Committee is of the opinion that this is a major shortcoming in the port sector. The
Consent to Operate for Ports is a necessary instrument. With the expansion of the Sagarmala
Project, this will be a necessity for small riverine docks that will come up as result of this project.
This is a flaw that must be remedied at the earliest as it leaves the Ports vulnerable to unnecessary
litigation and law suits. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping
must coordinate with the concerned Ministries and Agencies and format a 'Consent to Operate'
specifically for Ports at the earliest. (Para 271)
PUBLIC PRIV ATE PARTNERSHIPS (PPP)
The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of Shipping towards the development of
port infrastructure through the PPP model. The Committee recommends that as far as possible,
the same model must be utilised in all the Major Ports to ensure the development of Port
infrastructure in the country. Steps must be taken in tandem with the State Governments
concerned in order to ensure smooth and speedy implementation of the PPP projects.
(Para 276)
DEVELOPMENT/ PROMOTION OF CRUISE FACILITIES AT PORTS
The Committee is pleased to note the proactive steps taken by the Ministry of Shipping in
tandem with the Major Ports to promote Cruise tourism in the nation. With the growing population

74
and infrastructure constraints especially in city based Major Ports, the Committee is of the view
that Cruise Shipping is an important and viable alternative to help promote the growth of the
economy by way of tourism in the country. The Committee further recommends that given the
nascent stage of its development, the policies with regards to Cruise Shipping in the country
must be regularly updated and modified to keep in tune with the changing global economic
scenario. The Committee further recommends that taxation policies in this regard must be
formulated in a manner which helps facilitate its growth. (Para 279)
The Committee was informed that charging cruise ships on the basis of their tonnage,
rather than on the number of passengers, is a dampner. The Committee recommends that cruise
terminals may be developed in all the city based ports to attract foreign licenses and promote
cruise tourism. (Para 280)
PROMOTION OF RO-RO OPERATIONS
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry of Shipping in developing RoRo
operations and services in the country. The Committee, however, feels that more needs to be
done as Ro-Ro services are integral to the economic prosperity of the nation and serve as a
wonderful means of transport by utilizing the inland waterways in the country. In this regard,
the Committee recommends that the Ministry must pick up the speed of the Sagarmala Project
in order to make it viable and operational in the country. This will go a long way in improving
the hinterland connectivity, reducing transport costs and reducing travel time in terms of cargo
management in the country. (Para 282)
PROMOTION OF SOLAR ENERGY GENERATION
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Major Ports should make use of the large
tracts of unused land available to them in order to ensure the implementation of the Green Port
Initiative. Apart from being an efficient way of utilizing the space available, the income generated
from the sale of the energy generated can be used to further augment the development of the
Port and its ancillary services. (Para 286)
ECOLOGICAL CONSIDERATIONS
The Ports also have a certain responsibility to ensure the sustainability of the ecological
resources that surround them. The Committee strongly feels that it is the responsibility of the
Port Authorities and the Ministry of Shipping by extension to nurture and preserve the environment.
The recent reports of recurrent oil spills are a cause of concern for the flora and fauna and the
environment in general. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping
must ensure that the Ports have set guidelines to prevent incidents of oil spills in the future and
steps must be taken to ensure that the oil spills are cleaned up. Promotion of eco-friendly
business is the need of the hour and must be considered an important parameter when considering
the annual performance of a port. This must also extend to the private and small ports as well,
as a matter of policy. (Para 287)

of operational cost and profit, he explained that the high operational cost was only due to the pensions
that were paid to its employees.
7. He further stated that a part of the plan of reinventing itself also included handling cargo only for
the Mumbai city limits. Plans have also been made for a floating storage and re-gasification unit through
LNG. Moreover, construction of bunkering terminal has been completed; this is a venture that is a major
business in countries like Singapore and MbPT is entering this business now. The Indra Port which is
a dry dock under MbPT was facing certain issues. The Port has since signed an MoU with Cochin
Shipyard for the latter to take over the ship-repair operations, for which they are to be paid ` 14 crores.
A modern fishing harbour at Sassoon dock is also planned. An East-to-West trans-harbour link is also
in the pipeline. The Committee noted that no proper timelines have been given and have requested for
the same. Also, water transport for the Mumbai city on the Eastern side, going from Mumbai to Navi
Mumbai to Nerul and from Mumbai to Mandwa is planned. The Committee noted that no proper timelines
have been given and have requested for the same which would cut down travel time between Mumbai
and Goa.
8. The Chairman of MbPT proceeded to elaborate on the plans for a Port terminal dedicated to Cruise.
He stated that the suggestions put forth in the report by Bermello and Ajamil were being implemented.
A major hindrance was the issue of Customs and taxation which were being resolved by the Ministry
of Shipping with the Department of Revenue. A Monitoring Committee has been constituted to oversee
the development of the Cruise terminal which is looking into the parameters of ease of doing business.
To facilitate the Cruise Terminal, a new International Cruise Terminal is being constructed inside the
Mumbai Port premises itself which is expected to be completed by mid- next year. He informed the
Committee that efforts are also being made to build relations with the 5 major cruise operators in the
world in order to encourage home- porting. Simultaneously, a Marina and a Jetti are being developed,
similar to those in Miami, Bussan and Vancouver. These run parallel to the Cruise business and help boost
its growth.
9. Thereafter, the Chairman -in-charge of Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) presented a brief
background on Jawaharlal Nehru Port. He stated that JNPT is one of the youngest ports consisting of
four terminals occupying an area of 3,052 acres. Of the four ports, one is Jawaharlal Nehru Port
Container Terminal (JNPCT) which is run by the Port Authority itself, the others are run by Dubai Ports
World (DP World), Gateway Terminals India (GTI) and recently, the Port of Singapore Authority's port
has been commissioned. The current market share of JNPT is 53 per cent of Major Port container traffic
and is ranked 33r amongst the top 100 Container terminals world over and is expected to join the 10
million Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit (TEU) club in five years. The Port handled a record cargo of
66 million tonnes in the previous year, the highest ever in the history of JNPT. It recorded a growth
of 7.41 per cent and handled a record of 4.83 million TEUs of container cargo.

83
10. He then proceeded to elaborate on the operational logistics of the Port. JNPT, following the orders
of the Ministry of Shipping, has slowly shifted its operations towards Direct Port Delivery System (DPD)
for imports and Direct Port Export System (DPE) for exports and is reaping its rewards. Through the
DPD, an importer can pick up the container directly from the Port instead of routing it through the
Container Freight System (CFS) agents. This has reaped rich dividends and has resulted in economic
benefits. On the export side, the DPE has facilitated for export containers to reach the Port directly. He
explained that the practice has resulted in a significant reduction of Dwell Time, 112 hours reduced to
50 hours for imports to exit the port gate and similarly, it has been reduced to 83 hours for exports.
This includes cargo aggregation time and the eight hours required for planning and loading time. Further,
he informed the Committee that steps are being taken to convert the Container Freight Company's (CFC)
spaces into warehouses and convert their services into those of warehousing facilities, to solve the
problem of floor space index and issues of space constraints.
11. He informed the Committee of the status of the modernization of the Jawaharlal Nehru Port. He
apprised the Committee that Inter-terminal movement of Tractor Trailers has been initiated in order to
decongest the Port traffic. RFID based Gate Automation system has been implemented where a truck
which enters to deposit a box, picks up an export box on its way back, saving a distance of seven-and-
a-half kilometer. Parallel to this, parking zones have been created in the Port. Parking has been allotted
to individual terminals and it has been made mandatory for the trucks to use the respective parking. The
rates have been kept minimal, at `60 for eight hours to facilitate parking and this has gone a long way
in regulating the traffic. The Customs have also been brought to the parking area so that the document
processing is done in the parking area itself before they enter the Port. A 45-hectare centralized parking
plaza is under construction. The plan is to place the best player in the operational area where each truck
would come. This place will be equipped with a central Customs office, restaurants, dormitories, medical
facilities etc. All regulatory agencies' laboratories would also be housed here to ensure that all shipment
requirements are placed under one roof.
12. While elaborating on the operational performance of the Port, the Chairman of JNPT stated that the
Average Parcel Size at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Container Terminal (JNPCT) has increased to 3,532 TEUs
against the average of 2,727 TEUs of JNPT. This has resulted in increased productivity due to decreased
berthing and un-berthing times and the increase in response time has reposed confidence in the terminal
among the efficient shipping lines. Furthermore, the Pre-Berthing Delay has been reduced and Average
Berth Productivity has increased, thus, resulting in increased container terminal efficiency.
13. The Committee was informed that a unique concept of Dry Port is being introduced to facilitate
cargo-aggregation. Wardha, Jalna, Nasik and Sangli have been identified as the four stations in Maharashtra.
These will act as stations of the ports in the hinterland, where the value of the shipment will be
calculated. Future projects similar to this will be undertaken for areas that share connectivity with JNPT.
However, the connectivity of rail, road and dependence upon JNPT are critical factors for this to be a
success. This will greatly reduce the cost incurred during stuffing to improve connectivity to the
hinterland. DFCC projects including the Western DFC from Dadri to JNPT (1,504) K.m. and the Eastern
DFC from Ludhiana to WB (1,856 K.m.), are also underway and are expected to be completed by June
2019.

84
14. The Committee was apprised that JNPT is promoting a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) of 277
Hectares which would provide key advantages towards promotion of Shore based manufacturing, Plug
and Play, Common infrastructure provision etc. This SEZ is ideal for Import- process and Export format
and will be benefitted by its proximity to Industrial Clusters and Multi-modal connectivity. The role of
JNPT in developing the Container Handling Facilities at Chabahar Port in Iran, through an MoU signed
between the two countries will greatly boost economic activity in the Port.
15. Furthermore, the Chairman-in-charge of JNPT stated that following the direction from the Ministry
of Shipping, the paperwork related to issuing delivery orders has been moved to an e-platform. It is now
an e-invoice, e-payment and e-delivery, and this has been made mandatory. This move, whilst improving
efficiency, has also led to the creation of logistic data banks. JNPT is now a paperless port and all
documentation is processed through a web-based portal. The Custom SEZ has been integrated with the
port system to facilitate the exchange of critical messages and hard copies are not required. He stated
that tariff of shipping lines have been made available online on the JNPT website. Moreover, efforts have
been made to shift container evacuation from road to rail. The rates of road and rail have been equalized
and the gate window time has been reduced from four to three days. He also stated that JNPT is working
with the National Cyber Cell in order to prevent threats to its cyber security. The Indian Ports Association
(IPA) has taken a lead in that to ensure that all twelve major ports have similar kind of cyber security.

2. The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee to the meeting. He informed them that the
agenda of the Committee is to hear the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping and the Chairmen of the Chennai
Port Trust, Kamarajar Port Limited, Cochin Port Trust, V .O. Chidambaranar Port Trust, Deendayal Port
Trust, Mormugao Port Trust, New Mangalore Port Trust and Visakhapatnam Port Trust on the subject
'Cargo Handling in Major Ports'.
3. The Chairman, V .O. Chidambaranar Port Trust informed the Committee that the Port is strategically
located on the international sea route and that steps are being taken to develop the Port as an international
trans-shipment hub. He apprised the Committee that the Port has 15 berths and that the channel is around
3.8 k.m. long. He stated that one of the main issues in the Port is the small entrance of around 153m
and that it is getting widened. While elaborating upon the cargo handling capacity of the Port, he stated
that the Port handled around 10-11 million tonnes thermal coal in 2017-18 and that 6.98 lakh Twenty
Foot Equivalent Units (TEUs) containers were handled in 2017-18. He drew attention of the Committee
to the policy initiative taken by the Ministry of Shipping in relaxing cabotage loss wherein foreign
shipping lines have been allowed to carry coastal cargo. He further stated that one state-of-the art truck
parking terminal and a full fledged Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) system have been introduced
in the Port.
4. The Secretary, Ministry of Shipping elucidated upon the steps taken to bring the cargo back to
Indian ports. He stated that foreign lines are now allowed to move cargo within Indian ports and that
the restrictions on Indian companies to charter foreign lines have been removed.
5. The Chairman, Chennai Port Trust apprised the Committee that the Port mainly handles containers,
liquid bulk, dry bulk and break bulk. He stated that the Port has 24 berths which handle about 52 million
tonnes of cargo and that the port has automobile cargo handled in Ro-Ro ships. He also stated that the
roads inside the Port have been widened and laned and that the gate complex has been modernised. He
informed the Committee that investment has been made in creation of rail facility inside the Port and that
a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was entered with Puducherry Government to develop Puducherry
Port as a satellite port.
6. The CMD, Kamarajar Port Limited, while making the presentation, stated that the Port is a landlord
port and that the Port has eight terminals. He further stated that all the terminals are equipped with state-
of-the-art infrastructure facilities with fully mechanized cargo handling operations for faster evacuation
and that the Port has got excellent rail connectivity. He narrated the steps being taken to improve road
connectivity of the Port and informed the Committee that a state-of-the-art cruise terminal has been set
up at Chennai Port.

88
7. The Chairman, Cochin Port Trust informed the Committee that in 2017-18, the Port handled 29.38
million metric tones (MMT) as against the target of 28.5 MMT. He apprised the Committee that the
average pre-berthing detention time was 7.61 hours in 2018 and that the average turn around time was
1.46 days in 2018. He explained the healthy sustainable growth of the Port in terms of container volume.
He stated that drive-through scanners which can scan around 60 trucks in one hour have been installed
and that the trucks which enter the International Container Transshipment Terminal (ICTT) can leave the
facility in 27 minutes.
8. The Chairman, Deendayal Port Trust informed the Committee that the traffic handled by the Port
in the last year was 105 metric tons (MT) and that the profit and the operating income have nearly
doubled in the last 5 years. He apprised the Committee that the existing berths in the Port are 31 and
that 10 more are being added. He explained to the Committee that development of cargo berth number
14 and berth number 16 have been taken up and that construction of oil jetty number 7 has also been
taken up.
9. The Chairman, Mormugao Port Trust informed the Committee that the iron ore leases in Goa have
been cancelled by the Supreme Court and that it has impacted the cargo exports of the Port. He explained
to the Committee that 20 million tonnes of iron ore was handled by the Port in a year and that cargo
would not be available from 2018. The issue is being dealt at the State Government level.
10. The Chairman, Visakhapatnam Port Trust while highlighting the major features of the Port, stated
that it is the only major port with 18.1 m draft which can handle super cape size vessels with 2 lakh
Dead Weight Tonnage (DWT) category and that it is the deepest container terminal among all the major
ports with 16.5 m draft. He informed the Committee that the Port runs entirely on solar energy and the
entire water requirement of the Port, except potable water, is taken from sewage treatment. He apprised
the Committee that in the last 5 years, an investment of around ` 1052 crores was made on new
terminals and mechanisation and that ` 510 crores was spent on deepening of channels and berths.
11. The Chairman, New Mangalore Port Trust informed the Committee that the Port has entered into
an agreement with Chettinad for development of coal terminal of 6 million tonnes costing ` 469.46 crores
and that the construction of 1.2 millions of litres per day (MLD) sewage treatment plant has been
completed. He pointed out that one of the bottlenecks faced by the Port is its limited water front and
stated that the growth of container traffic has been almost 23% for the last four years. He apprised the
Committee that the cost of the land based 4 mega watt (MW) solar plant was ` 24 crores and that the
cost of the roof top 1.2 MW solar plant was ` 6 crores.
12. The Chairman of the Committee desired that the Ministry of Shipping may furnish a detailed note
on the issues given below, within a week's time:
• Steps to be taken by the ports to become competitive with International ports such as
Singapore, Colombo and Jebel Ali;
• Public Private Partnership in the ports;
• Alternatives in the wake of closure of the Sterlite company in Tamil Nadu;
• Using the economies of scale;

• Ro Ro facility;

• Steps being taken and desired steps to prevent oil spills;
• Steps taken by various Ports and the Ministry of Shipping to promote cruise tourism and
cruise ships;
• National Green Tribunal (NGT) order as a result of which a number of projects of various
ports were put on hold;
• Latest financial figures of the Ports; and

I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Two

REPORT
Jammu and Kashmir holds a special place in the collective hearts of the nation. This picturesque
State nestled amidst the Himalayas holds the captive imagination of the country as a ‘paradise on
earth’. Images of its pristine landscape, house boats on the Dal Lake, lush valleys, the deep blue
lakes springing forth from Himalayan glaciers, the stark bareness of the cold deserts of Leh have
been etched in the minds of generations of Indians. Scenic shots of Leh etc. have captured the
beauty of Jammu & Kashmir in full cinematic glory, making Jammu and Kashmir an alluring
destination, to be visited by tourists, both domestic and international.
2. The tourism industry in Jammu and Kashmir is known across the world for its scenic landscape,
beautiful valleys, lakes, snowcapped mountains and religious places. The State of Jammu and Kashmir has
three distinct regions viz., Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh. All the three regions have immense potential for
tourism from both domestic as well as international tourists. Its impact is visible in the service industry
sectors such as transport, hospitality, horticulture, handicraft and the small scale industry.
3. With the Himalayas as its background, Kashmir’s natural landscape has made it a popular destination
for adventure tourism in South Asia. Jammu is renowned for its ancient temples, Hindu shrines, gardens and
forts. The Hindu holy shrine of Amarnath in Kashmir attracts millions of Hindu devotees every year, as does
the Vaishno Devi shrine in Jammu region. Jammu’s historic monuments feature a unique blend of Islamic
and Hindu architectural styles. Ladakh, the third region of the State has emerged as a major hub for adventure
and eco-tourism. This part of the Greater Himalayas popularly called ‘Moon on Earth’ comprises of naked
peaks and deep gorges. It was once an integral part of the silk route to Asia from the subcontinent.
4. Given its mountainous terrain and landlocked location, tourism is the primary economic activity of the
State and is the bread earner for a major part of the State. Jammu and Kashmir largely depends on the natural
resources that this place has to offer. Visitors’ spending generate income for both public and private sectors,
besides generating employment opportunities. Given that tourism is integral to the development of the State
of Jammu & Kashmir, the Committee decided to take up the subject ‘Development of Tourism in Jammu &
Kashmir’ for examination and report thereon.
5. In this connection, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism
and Culture heard the views of the Ministry of Tourism; State Government of Jammu and Kashmir; and
Travel and Tour operators, Hoteliers etc. on the subject at Srinagar on 25th June, 2016. The Committee also
heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism; Ministry of Finance; and State Government of
Jammu and Kashmir on the subject at Delhi on 14th July, 2016. The Committee further heard the views of
the Ministry of Tourism; State Government of Jammu and Kashmir; and Travel and Tour operators, Hoteliers
etc. on the subject at Srinagar on 11th July, 2018.
6. Some of the major points discussed during the deliberations of the Committee are: -

(ii) Distribution of Funds
(iii) Seasonality

STATE TOURISM POLICY
7. A State Tourism Policy is essential to ensure the planned development of tourism in the region. The
Committee was informed by the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism that States have been encouraged to formulate
a State Policy for tourism to give direction to the growth of tourism in the State and to ensure its sustainability
in the years to come. The Committee was informed by the representatives of the State Government of
Jammu & Kashmir in July, 2018 that the State had formulated a State Tourism Policy which was being
finalised.
8. The Committee feels that the formulation of State Tourism Policy is integral to the growth,
promotions and sustenance of tourism and related activities in the region. The Tourism Policy
should give equal opportunities to all the stakeholders involved in tourism related activities like
the local people, private sector and NGOs. It should include provisions to promote effective
communication and greater intra-State coordination within J&K, i.e., Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh.
As tourism is mainly a private sector driven industry, it is important for J&K Government to act as
a facilitator with respect to tourism. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism, Government of India should pursue with the  State Government  to finalise the State
Tourism Policy at the earliest. The Committee further recommends that the State Tourism Policy,
upon release, must be placed in public domain.
9. The Committee may be informed of the details of historical monuments and heritage sites in
J&K and the maintenance of the UNESCO Heritage Sites in the State. The Committee may also be
apprised of the present condition of the Pari Mahal. The Committee recommends that the same
may be included in the Action Taken Replies.
DISTRIBUTION OF FUNDS
10. The Comm ittee was informed by the Ministry of Tourism about the various policies which have
been introduced to provide funding towards the development of Swadesh Darshan (Annexure-I) for
integrated development of tourism based theme circuits and PRASHAD in Jammu & Kashmir (Annexure-V).
It was stated that there have been limited allocation of funds under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme.
However, given its status, the State has been allocated special funds under Prime Minister Development
Plan (2016) (Annexure-IV) .
11. It has been brought to the attention of the Committee that the State Government of J&K has not
submitted any proposals for funds during 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 for the development of tourism in

3
Ladakh region under the PRASHAD/Swadesh Darshan. Furthermore, the Committee was informed that
there have been no proposals for projects under Buddhist Circuit in Ladakh.
12. The Committee expresses its displeasure that the State Government has not submitted any
proposals for the development of tourism in Ladakh region continuously for two years. The Committee
reiterates its view that development of tourism is integral to the holistic development of the State.J
& K deserves to be prosperous and economically able, to ensure a better life for its residents. The
Committee urges upon the State of J&K to submit proposals for the development of tourism in
Ladakh region, at the earliest. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism must coordinate with the State Government to ensure that sufficient funds and due publicity
are given for the promotion of tourism in Ladakh region.
13. As Ladakh region offers multiple tourism options which cater to the taste of a vast array of
tourists from varied age groups, the Committee recommends that an elaborate tourism development
plan should be conceived for Ladakh which accounts for focussed  promotion of rural, theme based
and adventure tourism, besides opening of new destinations for the tourists.
SEASONALITY
14. The Committee is aware that in Jammu and Kashmir, every year, there is a shift of the Secretariat and
all other Government offices, from Srinagar to Jammu and vice versa . This bi-annual shift is known as
‘Darbar’ move. From May to October, all Government offices are housed in Srinagar which is the summer
capital of the State and from November to April, the offices are housed in Jammu which is the winter capital
of the State. The Jammu and Kashmir High Court also moves from Srinagar to Jammu in winters and from
Jammu to Srinagar in summers.
15. Jammu & Kashmir is blessed with temperate climate with four distinct seasons. Due to its geographical
position, most parts of the State are inundated with snow. This becomes a major drawback in the development
of capital infrastructure in the region.  The Committee was informed that the working season in the region
is extremely short and limited, given the terrain of the region, administrative difficulties and lack of advanced
machinery in the region, resulting in delay in completion of projects.
16. The Committee understands that the seasonality of the region, along with the other variables,
may contribute to the delay in completion of projects in the region. The Committee is of the view
that the time table followed by the Ministry of Finance towards funding various activities in the
region may not be conducive to the peculiarities of the region. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and other
stakeholders may  impress upon the Ministry of Finance to chalk out a plan to ensure a more
sustainable and efficient way of releasing funds to J&K and other similarly affected States.
CONNECTIVITY
(i)  Air
17. The Committee is pleased to note that the airports at Leh and Srinagar have been upgraded and made
functional (Annexure-V). The Association of Tour, Travel and Hotel operators of the State informed the
Committee that the exorbitant price of air tickets is a major dampener. Escalating airfares of ‘low cost’
carriers during the peak season are a major deterrent to increasing footfall in the region. The airfares are

4
equivalent to that of the nearby foreign destinations and given the sensitivity of the region, tourists would
prefer to visit nearby foreign destinations at the same airfare rather than visit J&K.
18. In this regard, the Committee recommends that necessary measures must taken to keep the
air fares for J & K during the peak tourist season, under reasonable limit. The Committee also
recommends that the number of flights from Srinagar to Leh and from Srinagar to Kargil may be
increased.
19. Given the mountainous terrain and the frequency of landslides in the region, the Committee
recommends that Pawan Hans Services may be further augmented by pressing additional helicopters
into service, for tourist facilitation, to lesser known destinations like Gurez, Bangus, Kishtwar and
Kargil. UDAN scheme should also be devised in such a manner as to connect Srinagar with other
major cities especially in the peak tourist season.
20. The Committee could understand that the Sheikh-ul-Alam Airport (International airport) at
Srinagar is not functional. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must initiate
talks with the Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Airports Authority of
India, to facilitate the operation of international flights from Srinagar. The Committee recommends
that the infrastructure provided at Srinagar Airport must be improved.
(ii)  Railways
21. Railways are an economical and romantic way of exploring the country.  Rail journeys are affordable
and increase the connectivity of the region with other parts of India. Domestic tourists are primarily train-
friendly and prefer to travel by trains due to better connectivity and affordability.
22. The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Tourism provided financial assistance to the tune of
12 crores @ ` 4 crore per coach to the Ministry of Railways for the manufacture of three glass top coaches,
for developing rail tourism in the country. The ‘Glass Top Coach’ have been designated for the route
between Budgam to Banihal and Baramulla to Srinagar.The Vistadome Coach boasts of a glass roof which
has electrically controlled opalescence, i.e., it can be made transparent or opaque at the turn of a switch –
360 degree rotatable, pushback chairs and automatic shading compartment doors.
23. The Committee recommends that Tourist Trains may be introduced to J&K from various
metros of the country. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must
coordinate with the Ministry of Railways for better railway connectivity with the valley, besides
operating additional tourist trains from all Metro Cities to J & K. Furthermore, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must coordinate with the Ministry of Railways to facilitate
the speedy completion of the Vistadome Coaches. These Coaches, with the glass tops, would be a
wonderful addition to the railway services in the region, by giving its passengers a 360 degree view
of the surrounding regions.
(iii)  Road
24. Jammu & Kashmir is a place of religious prominence and a popular pilgrimage destination. However,
the conditions of the roads in the region leave much to be desired. The Committee understands that the
mountainous terrain of the region makes building of capital infrastructure a herculean task. Roads, thus,
serve to become the cheapest and most reliable mode of transportation.

5
25. The Committee, in this regard, notes that the region is prone to frequent landslides,  road caving etc.
Many of the tourists are forced to travel by foot, while carrying the old and disabled on hand held palanquins.
Moreover, the Committee noticed that the roads lack proper signages and safety markers at bends or around
the thinner mountainside roads.
26. The Committee strongly feels that the National Highways should take initiatives to improve
the roads in Jammu & Kashmir. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism may impress upon the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to expedite the upgradation
of Jammu-Srinagar highway which is long pending. Furthermore, the Ministry of Road Transport &
Highways, through its agencies in the region, may also coordinate with the concerned State
departments in order to ensure that the roads including the National Highways are properly
maintained; signageare put in place and to ensure that fluorescent safety markers are installed
along the roads to reduce the incidence of accidents in the region.
27. The Committee also recommends the Ministry of Tourism to impress upon the Ministry of
Road Transport & Highways and the Government of J&K to improve road infrastructure in pilgrim
and border towns and backward areas of the State where the road network is poor and the existing
roads are unable to cater to the ever increasing vehicular movement.
28. The Committee observes that for all the above mentioned works related to connectivity, no
timelines or follow up mechanisms are in place. Delays in completion of projects increase the costs
and woes of people. The Committee recommends that an effective mechanism may be set up to
ensure that the respective Ministries take these recommendations seriously and come up with
specific and concrete timelines to follow up on the progress made and funds utilized.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
29. The presence of trained and skilled workforce is necessary for the success of a destination as a tourist
destination. The Committee was informed of the dearth of trained individuals in the tourism sector in the
State. The Committee is pleased to note the construction of the Institute of Hotel Management (IHM) in
Srinagar. However, there is a lack of qualified and trained professionals in tourism management.
30. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must collaborate with the State
Government in order to introduce contemporary courses by the Indian Institute of Tourism and
Travel Management (IITTM) in the region. The students must be given due exposure in other
States. The Committee recommends that training must not be restricted to theoretical knowledge,
but must include internships and regular interactions with industry pioneers, in order to gauge the
present requirement of the sector. Local Universities and professional colleges should be encouraged
to introduce courses on Tourism studies and foreign language courses, in collaboration with national
and international institutes of Tourism studies.
31. The Committee recommends that the State Government may devise programs to introduce
skill/ craft as a subject under Socially Useful Productive Work (SUPW) in the curriculum, in order
to educate children of the rich traditional handicrafts of the State, develop skills in the State and
promote such activity. This will go a long way in ensuring a livelihood in the State, whilst ensuring
the longevity of these prized handicraft skills.
32. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must work with the Ministry

6
of Finance to provide some exemption to handicrafts under implementation of GST in order to
ensure a market for the handcrafted products which are presently being cornered by the cheaper
Chinese products.
MEDIA AND PROMOTION
33. The Committee was informed by the various stakeholders of tourism in the region that a major hindrance
to increasing the footfall in the region is the constant negative publicity received by the State as a troubled
State. This perception overshadows the true narrative of the region, as not all parts of the State are in
conflict or affected by it.
34. The Committee was also informed that the travel advisories issued by various countries acted as an
impediment in attracting foreign tourists. The Committee feels that many a times, the advisories are based
on ill-informed facts and unnecessary assessment of local conditions. The Committee feels that the print
and electronic media, both domestic and international, have an important role in projecting the favourable
situations existing in J & K.
35. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should organize their
own publicity campaign in order to remove the negative impression which are based on incorrect
facts. The Ministry should also involve the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the Ministry
of External Affairs for the removal of advisories imposed by various countries against travel to
Jammu & Kashmir.
36. The Committee recommends that the State Government, Ministry of Tourism and the various
other stakeholders must endeavor to remove the negative publicity in the press by finding innovative
means to engage with the world at large via the social media. In this age of Youtube and social
platforms like Instagram and Snapchat, social media influencers may be engaged to promote a
more positive image of the State. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the State
Government must engage with ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI to invite and encourage companies to
host meetings and visits in the region. The Committee feels that websites of the Ministry of Tourism
and its various arms should be made interactive and user-friendly. Mobile applications and social
networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Snapchat, Instagram etc. should be harnessed as a quick
and cost effective medium for tourism marketing.
BUDDHIST CIRCUIT
37. The Committee could understand that the Ladakh region of the State is predominantly Buddhist.
However, it was informed that the Leh and Ladakh region of the State have not been included in the purview
of the Buddhist Circuit. The Committee feels that the Buddhist Circuit is integral to the promotion of the soft
power of India via its culture. The scenic landscape and terrain are a perfect backdrop for the Buddhist
Festivals in the region which are a major tourist attraction and are very popular the world over.
38. The Committee recommends that the State Government must take efforts to co-ordinate
with the Ministry of Tourism, in order to include Ladakh and Leh under the Buddhist Circuit in the
country and develop the tourist destinations in the region.
TOURIST FACILITIES
39. The Committee observed during its visit to Jammu and Kashmir that the State requires further

7
input in terms of improving upon tourist facilities in the region. The tourist destinations must be
equipped with safe drinking water stations, clean and hygienic washrooms, rest stop, car stops etc.
The Committee recommends that tourist facilities proposed under the Swadesh Darshan scheme
must be completed at the earliest. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the State
Government must put in place a system to ensure that these tourist amenities, once operational,
are well maintained and at par with global standards. The creation of adequate and suitable
infrastructure in terms of accommodation, transport, communication links etc. and other essential
amenities are the foundation for the success of tourism in the State.
40. The Committee recommends that in order to improve the maintenance of existing tourist
destinations, adoption/management/sponsorship programs should be promoted so as to create a
sense of ownership in the minds of locals and corporates alike, for monuments, religious sites and
tourist destinations.
41. During the visit of the Committee to Srinagar, it was informed that there was an urgent need
to introduce a Laser Show on the Dal Lake and restart the Sound and Light Show at Shalimar
Gardens. The Committee may be apprised of the status of implementation of the Sound and Light
Show at Dal Lake. The Committee feels that these facilities may definitely attract more tourists
while serving to narrate the story of Kashmir. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism should extend financial support to the Government of J & K to restart the above mentioned
projects.
SAFETY OF TOURISTS
42. Safe and secure travel is always the top priority for travelers. The Committee feels that security of
tourists must be given top priority. The Committee was informed by the Tour and travel operators and
Hoteliers that the travel bans imposed by various Governments, both international and domestic on travel to
the State create an air of negativity in the region. The Committee, during its visit to Srinagar, observed
that the situation was more peaceful than what was reported in the news and media. The Committee
feels that this is a matter which must be broached with caution as it involves issues of national
security.
43. The popularity of the region as a ‘dham’ pilgrimage site is offset by large crowds travelling on foot.
Often, the elderly, women and children have to be carried on indigenous palanquins which are neither sturdy
nor reliable.  The result is a chaotic situation of unregulated crowds which cause regular stampedes which
leave many injured and prove fatal for others.
44. The Committee, in this regard, recommends that the State Government must work on crowd
management in coordination with the concerned temple authorities, to formulate a plan to regulate
the crowds in the area. Furthermore, the State Government of J&K must work to ensure the
provision of regulated assistance, in order to prevent overcrowding by vendors.
45. The Committee recommends that the State Government must endeavour to establish an
evacuation plan and procedure, with signage and instructions at regular intervals, to help and evacuate
the tourists in the event of a stampede or a natural calamity.
46. The Committee is pleased to note that the State Government has implemented Tourism
Police in the State. The Committee recommends that the Tourism Police must be trained regularly

8
and must undergo sensitization training to deal with the large number of tourists arriving from
different countries, cultures and languages. The Committee desires that the Tourist Police may
also be encouraged to learn foreign languages in order to better serve foreign tourists in the
region.
SAFETY ALERTS
47. The Committee notes that the region is prone to natural calamities and feels that the State must be
better equipped to handle situations in the event of calamities, both natural and man-made.
48. In this regard, the Committee strongly feels that the State Government must work towards
ensuring the safety of tourists in the region. The Committee recommends that the State Government
must work to ensure that its volunteers, Tourist Police and State Police are regularly trained by the
National Disaster Relief Force (NDRF) in the evacuation and rescue of civilians. The Committee
further recommends that the State Government must work to coordinate regular joint exercises
with the volunteers, Army and the NDRF in preparation for any eventualities.
ECOLOGICAL SUSTAINABILITY
49. The Co mmittee was informed by the stakeholders that J&K has been declared a fragile Eco Zone.
The Committee notes that pollution and waste management are problems being faced by the J & K
Government.
50. The Committee recommends that the State Government of Jammu & Kashmir must envisage
a Solid Waste treatment plant in Srinagar and other prominent tourist destinations. The State must
work to clean up the Dal Lake, Nigeen Lake and develop the Wular Lake. Solar Energy must be
encouraged in the region and green initiatives must be undertaken. The Committee recommends
that the State should draw up an action plan on how to maintain cleanliness and develop and maintain
an ecologically – friendly and ecologically – viable form of tourism in the region.
51. The Committee feels that the State Government needs to regulate the houseboat operations
on the Dal Lake keeping in mind its carrying capacity and introduce special incentives to start
houseboat operations in areas other than Dal and Nageen Lakes.
52. The Committee feels that special efforts should be taken to highlight famous lakes of the
State in order to promote them as important tourist destinations as a part of eco-tourism in the
State. Steps should be taken to preserve and enhance their beauty by undertaking development in
an integrated manner. Moreover, Lakes and Waterways Development Authority (LWDA) must
ensure that wastes generated by houseboats are not dumped into the lakes. Furthermore, emphasis
should be placed on the introduction of an effective Waste Management Treatment System.
Goods and Services Tax
53. The sensitive nature of Jammu & Kashmir must be taken into consideration during the development of
tourism in the region. The implementation of GST on tourism in the region would have manifold effects,
mostly negative on the economy of the region. The Committee was informed by the stakeholders that
sourcing of products and materials is an issue. Unlike other States, the residents of Jammu & Kashmir and
its business owners spend huge amounts of money on procuring essentials, most of which have to be flown
in, which increases their capital expenditure. Most wholesale traders insist on payment in cash which is a

9
major issue, as the support from the Government must be processed viathe  Public Financial Management
System (PFMS) payment system which insists on digital transactions.
54. Furthermore, the Committee was informed that small business owners for small scale hotels, bed and
breakfasts and home stays cannot list their properties on various travel intermediary websites as there is a
levy of an 18percent of GST, which cuts across the little profit that they might make, making their venture
unsustainable.
55. In this regard, the Committee recommends that the implementation of GST on tourism related
activities in the State must be reconsidered. It must be done in a cautious and phased manner in
order to ensure that the delicate state of tourism in the region is not adversely affected. Furthermore,
the Committee suggests that the Ministry of Tourism must initiate dialogues with the  Ministry of
Finance in order to formulate a policy wherein tourism in the region can be supported and developed
over a period by giving tax sops for a given time period and to be leaned off slowly, in order to
ensure the sustained development of the region.
NEED FOR GREATERCENTRE- STATE COORDINATION
56. The development of J&K has been integral to the overall development policy for the nation. In this
regard, the Committee was informed that the Prime Minister’s Reconstruction Package (PMRP) was instituted
as early as 2004 and a great deal of money was sanctioned under different kind of projects which included
a project for rural tourism, tourism authorities and one for the Circuits amongst others. The Committee was
further informed that the package also included compensation for businesses destroyed/ damaged by the
floods in 2014.
57. The Committee was also informed that under the Product/Infrastructure Development For Destinations
and Circuits, the Ministry of Tourism extended Central Financial Assistance to the State Governments/Union
Territory administrations for tourism projects identified in consultation with them for the improvement of
existing tourism products and also for developing new ones. Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of
Product/Infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits, 100%  Central assistance is given for
development of destinations/circuits, including mega projects, to world standard and also for Rural Tourism
infrastructure development. The Ministry of Tourism provides financial assistance up to ` 5.00 crore for the
development of destinations and ` 8.00 crore for circuits. The upper limit of financial assistance has been
increased to ` 25 crore and ` 50 crore for development of identified mega destinations and circuits respectively,
under the schemes to promote rural tourism in the country. The thrust is for development of tourism
infrastructure at the identified rural tourism sites so that socio-economic benefits percolate down to the
rural community. A maximum of ` 50.00 lakhs is sanctioned for each project under this scheme for
development of tourism related infrastructure. The Committee was informed that the scheme had been
restructured under PRASHAD and Swadesh Darshan. The details of amount sanctioned and funds provided
under the Swadesh Darshan have been included in Annexure I. The details of amount sanctioned and the
funds provided under the PRASHAD are provided in Annexure III.
58. Upon scrutiny of the subject, the Committee is of the opinion that there is a major lacuna in
coordination and policy implementation between the Centre and State Government. Only a small
portion of the amount sanctioned has been released via Phase I and Phase II. Given the importance
of the State and its strategic position, the Committee emphasizes on greater coordination between
the Centre and the State Government.

10
59. The Committee notes that a large number of projects which have been funded under the
Central Government Schemes are yet to be completed. The Committee has observed that there
seems to be a lacuna in communication with regards to funding of these projects. The Committee
feels that this is due to a lack of coordination between the State and Central Governments and the
implementing agencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should
take greater initiative and facilitate communication between the various Central Government
agencies and the State Government (including the Department of Tourism) in order to ensure
smooth and timely implementation of the projects. The Committee further recommends that a
‘Coordination Committee’ must be constituted, spearheaded by the Ministry of Tourism, which
would include the State Government agencies and the Central Government agencies who are
stakeholders in the projects. This would go a long way to ensure that there is a common platform to
facilitate and coordinate various projects, while also serving to act as a monitoring Committee, to
monitor the implementation and progress of the projects.
SUBMISSION OF UTILISATION CERTIFICATES
60. The Committee is dismayed to note the disappointingly low percentage of submission of utilization
certificates by the State Government. The submission of utilisation certificates is essential to facilitate the
release of funds for the proceeding phase of the respective projects. The Committee was informed that the
State Government has been lackadaisical in its submission of utilisation certificates for projects under
implementation, while at the same time, requesting for the release of funds for the proceeding stage.
61. The Committee acknowledges that the timely submission of utilisation certificates is critical.
Not only does it act as a monitor for progress of a project, but also essential, since funds are
released in stages. The Committee strongly feels that tardiness in submission of these utilisation
certificates is indicative of a lack of accountability on the part of the State Government. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance,
must impress upon the State Government of J&K to ensure the timely submission of utilisation
certificates, as it is vital to the implementation of projects. The Committee further recommends
that the Ministry of Tourism must include the status of submission of utilisation certificates vis a vis
projects under implementation in the State and reasons for the low percentage of submission of
utilization certificates and remedial measures required for their speedy liquidation, in their Action
Taken Reply.
62. The completion of projects is essential, as an employment generator and a catalyst, to boost
the economy of the State, for which tourism is its primary source of income. The Committee is yet
to receive any information on the status of completion of projects under the Swadesh Darshan
scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism must impress upon
the State Government and its Departments, the importance of development of the projects under
its purview. The progress made on the same may be furnished in the Action Taken Reply.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
STATE TOURISM POLICY
The Committee feels that the formulation of State Tourism Policy is integral to the growth,
promotions and sustenance of tourism and related activities in the region. The Tourism Policy
should give equal opportunities to all the stakeholders involved in tourism related activities like
the local people, private sector and NGOs. It should include provisions to promote effective
communication and greater intra-State coordination within J&K, i.e., Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh.
As tourism is mainly a private sector driven industry, it is important for J&K Government to act as
a facilitator with respect to tourism. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism, Government of India should pursue with the State Government to finalise the State Tourism
Policy at the earliest. The Committee further recommends that the State Tourism Policy, upon
release, must be placed in public domain. (Para 8)
The Committee may be informed of the details of historical monuments and heritage sites in
J&K and the maintenance of the UNESCO Heritage Sites in the State. The Committee may also be
apprised of the present condition of the Pari Mahal. The Committee recommends that the same
may be included in the Action Taken Replies. (Para 9)
DISTRIBUTION OF FUNDS
The Committee expressed its displeasure that the State Government has not submitted any
proposals for the development of tourism in Ladakh region continuously for two years. The Committee
reiterates its view that development of tourism is integral to the holistic development of the State.
J & K deserves to be prosperous and economically able, to ensure a better life for its residents. The
Committee urges upon the State of J&K to submit proposals for the development of tourism in
Ladakh region, at the earliest. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Tourism must coordinate with the State Government to ensure that sufficient funds and due publicity
are given for the promotion of tourism in Ladakh region. (Para 12)
As Ladakh region offers multiple tourism options which cater to the taste of a vast array of
tourists from varied age groups, the Committee recommends that an elaborate tourism development
plan should be conceived for Ladakh which accounts for focussed  promotion of rural, theme based
and adventure tourism, besides opening of new destinations for the tourists. (Para 13)
SEASONALITY
The Commi ttee understands that the seasonality of the region, along with the other
variables, may contribute to the delay in completion of projects in the region. The Committee
is of the view that the time table followed by the Ministry of Finance towards funding various
activities in the region may not be conducive to the peculiarities of the region. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
and other stakeholders may impress upon the Ministry of Finance to chalk out a plan to ensure
a more sustainable and efficient way of releasing funds to J& K and other similarly affected
States. (Para 16)
